extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students conducting survey-based studies and SEM in mass communication (esp. studies of journalists/television news)
extracted.subtask_description: Methodological guidance for designing and administering a web survey of television reporters and for modeling influences on news content using hybrid structural equation models (SEM). Includes survey administration protocol, instrument operationalization, missing-data handling, scale construction, and SEM specification/identification procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reminder/contact protocol (five contacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three reminder messages were sent for a total of five contacts (postal mail pre-notification letter; e-mail invitation; and reminders one, two, and three).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule: first reminder seven days after initial e-mail (Wednesday, Feb. 21); second reminder approximately one week later; third reminder six days after second. Follow Dillman’s recommendation of personalizing messages — official invitation and reminders began with each respondent’s first name. Use survey software (Qualtrics) to track completions to avoid unnecessary messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted response rate and feasibility considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 30% targeted response rate for the current study was set given the larger sample (more than 600) and resource constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some e-mail studies achieve ~50% after many contacts/phone follow-ups, those involved smaller samples and different respondent roles; phone follow-ups were judged infeasible due to time and cost. Compare targeted response rates to similar studies (e.g., Pew Research) when justifying targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-notification and multimode options
rubrics_metrics.description: A mail pre-notification letter was sent to all sampled reporters; respondents could request a mail survey, and some opted for phone or fax completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a postage-paid return envelope for mail responses. Track undeliverable mail and adjust the possible sample accordingly (e.g., six returned as undeliverable reduced sample). Offer alternate modes to accommodate respondent preference and increase usable responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument length and pretesting
rubrics_metrics.description: The web survey consisted of 70 questions. A pretest of academics with extensive television experience was conducted and found the survey took an average of 13 minutes to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pretesting to check for ambiguities, word choice, and items that may deter completion; make minor wording adjustments based on pretest feedback. Do not include pretest data in analysis if specified (this study did not use pretest data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Likert-type formats and item ordering to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The survey used two main scale measures (Strongly Disagree/Strongly Agree and Almost Never/Very Often), both using a 7-point Likert-type format. In most instances, the questions were ordered so scale items did not appear continuously; some items were reverse-ordered to help prevent response bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermix scale items and reverse-code selected items to reduce response set bias. Ensure clear operational wording aimed at perceptions of typical newsrooms rather than strictly personal behavior to encourage candid responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of latent constructs and their indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Latent variables in the survey/model: (1) extramedia influences, (2) organizational influences, (3) within-media influences, and (4) content influence/outcome. Each latent construct is measured by multiple observed indicators (survey items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a mapping table of latent constructs to observed variables (as Table 3.1 does). Example indicators: extramedia → advertising, public relations, political pressures; organizational → level of concentration, owner/executive pressure, economic pressure; within-media → staff size pressure, direct management pressure, indirect management pressure; content outcomes → agenda building, frame building, agenda cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct measurement: reflective (effect) indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators were depicted as reflective (arrows from latent constructs to observed variables), meaning measured variables are effects of the latent constructs rather than causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose reflective representation when indicators are observable manifestations of an abstract construct. If arrows pointed from indicators to construct it would imply formative (causal) indicators, which was judged inappropriate for these constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale reliability assessment via Cronbach’s alpha
rubrics_metrics.description: Each multi-item scale was assessed for internal consistency using Cronbach’s alpha (e.g., advertising pressures alpha = .87; public relations pressures alpha = .81; political/governmental pressures alpha = .82; owner/executive pressures alpha = .94; level of ownership concentration alpha = .74; economic pressures alpha = .78; staff size pressure alpha = .68; direct management pressures alpha = .72; indirect management pressures alpha = .83; agenda building alpha = .80; frame building alpha = .80; agenda cutting alpha = .84).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report alpha, mean, and SD for scales. Use alpha to judge internal consistency and to guide item retention decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item retention and removal criteria (using alpha and squared multiple correlations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Items that reduced reliability/internal consistency or had low squared multiple correlations were removed from scales (examples: PR scale originally had five items; two were removed because they reduced alpha; political pressure items similarly reduced reliability and were dropped; owner/executive scale omitted an item with low squared multiple correlation; ownership concentration dropped an item that reduced alpha to .66; staff-size scale removed an item that reduced alpha to .44).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how each item affects Cronbach’s alpha and squared multiple correlations; remove items that degrade internal consistency or measure a different underlying concept. Retain items that contribute unique information even if they lower alpha slightly (document rationale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-size variable coding conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: DMA rank (market size) was reverse-coded in the model so that smaller DMA ranks represent smaller markets, and the variable was labeled 'Market Size' in the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly document any reverse coding to avoid confusion between descriptive tables and analytic variables; report both original and recoded representations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample inclusion/deletion rule for missingness (30% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only cases that had complete values for 9 of the 13 measured variables were retained. Cases missing values on more than 30% (five or more) of the variables were deleted, which led to deletion of 78 cases and 618 usable cases retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a predefined threshold for case-wise deletion based on proportion of missingness across measured variables; report number of dropped cases and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of missing-data mechanism and imputation
rubrics_metrics.description: After inspection, the data were considered missing at random (MAR). Because Maximum Likelihood estimation assumes no missing data, missing values were imputed using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm in EQS 6.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess missing-data patterns for MAR assumption. Use EM imputation for ML-based SEM when appropriate; justify method choice (e.g., cite comparative studies such as Gold & Bentler 2000 favoring EM regardless of missing-data proportion, distributional characteristics, or sample size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-screening procedures before SEM
rubrics_metrics.description: After imputing missing values, data were screened by examining descriptive statistics, checking for linearity, identifying outliers and/or extreme cases, and assessing the assumption of multivariate normality. The means and standard deviation values, minimum and maximum values, and bivariate scatterplots were examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure assumptions associated with SEM are met: linear relationships, acceptable ranges, absence of extreme outliers, and approximate multivariate normality. Document findings from screening and any corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEM procedural steps (Kline-derived workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kline’s recommended steps: specifying the model; model identification; selecting variables, operationalizing constructs, and screening/preparing the data file; model estimation; interpreting parameter estimates; considering equivalent models; re-specifying the model; interpreting and reporting the results. Additionally, replicate results in future studies and apply findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow an a priori modeling approach grounded in theory and prior research. Use CFA for the measurement portion and structural modeling for relationships among latent constructs. Document each step and any model modifications with justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model identification checks and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Four commonly used precautions to help ensure identification: setting the metric for latent variables (fix a loading to 1.0 or set latent variance to 1.0), the 't-rule' (number of parameters to estimate must be ≤ number of sample variances and covariances), local identification/three-indicator rule (three or more indicators per latent variable helps identification), and the recursive rule (no feedback loops/correlated errors ensures identification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these checks: set a metric (commonly fix one path to 1.0); compute known sample moments vs unknown parameters (t-rule); ensure, where possible, ≥3 indicators per latent construct but note identification can still hold with fewer; prefer recursive specifications to simplify identification. Example: hypothesized model had 13 observed measures → 91 sample moments and 28 parameters → overidentified with 63 df.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hybrid SEM models (latent + measured variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid models consist of both latent factors and measured variables; SEM separates into measurement (CFA) and structural portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict measurement model (how indicators load on latent factors) and structural model (how latent factors relate to each other). Use software with graphical interface (e.g., AMOS, EQS) to draw and estimate hybrid models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size guidance for SEM and split-sample model development
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule of thumb: have approximately 10 cases per parameter to estimate. Because the study used a model-development approach splitting the data into two subfiles (one for exploring/modifying and the other for confirming), a larger sample was required (280 cases needed per file; thus 560 needed total). The study had 618 usable cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning SEM with model building and cross-validation, multiply the usual sample-size rule by the number of subfiles. Report calculations showing adequacy of sample size relative to parameters to estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of items that measure different aspects (retain when informative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some items that reduced scale reliability were retained separately because they measured different aspects and contributed information (e.g., a political pressure item with a lower squared multiple correlation was retained because it measured a different aspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically drop items solely on alpha; inspect content and squared multiple correlations to determine whether an item measures a distinct concept worth keeping for future analyses. Document rationale for retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of reflective vs formative indicator choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators were depicted as reflective because they represent ways of measuring the unobservable constructs; the latent constructs were not treated as composites or indexes of the indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether indicators are effects (reflective) or causes (formative) of the latent construct, justify choice conceptually, and depict model arrows accordingly. Cite methodological literature when clarifying choice.
